note: Proposed build order from the 1 November 2026 MVP plan. These are planned work, not implemented capabilities. Items in openDecisions are not yet agreed.

features.name: Agent harness baseline
features.description: Agents can start, verify and resume work in this repository from its instruction and state files.
acceptance: ./init.sh and ./init.sh --full run the documented verification and fail on errors.
The harness validator scores all five subsystems.
Harness files stay out of the published package and the deployed site.
features.evidence: 2026-11-01: ./init.sh --full exited 0 with 60/60 tests and 48/48 Chromium and WebKit browser tests. A misformatted file made ./init.sh exit 1. validate-harness scored 100/100, a structural score only. npm pack --dry-run listed 15 files, none of them harness files, and Vercel serves only public/. features.name: Customer, product and environment ownership
features.description: Replace operator-only site provisioning with persisted ownership in the hierarchy account, product, environment, enforced on every product, environment, settings and telemetry query. Each environment holds its own site ID, server secret and allowed origins, so production, beta, staging and dev analytics stay separate.
acceptance: Two independent customers can create products and receive different configuration.
Neither customer can read or modify the other's products, environments or telemetry, at the API as well as the UI.
Demo and ticket-app installations keep working through the migration.
Sites and their origins load from the database, replacing the AGENT_ID_SITES environment variable.
Site secrets are encrypted at rest, because the collector must read them to sign.
A new product starts with a production environment. Beta, staging and dev environments can be added, each with its own site ID, server secret, origins and snippet.
An environment's type is fixed and its name is editable.

Environments are isolated within a customer: every event belongs to exactly one environment, dev traffic never reaches production's data, and one environment's site ID, secret or receipt never works for another.
decisions: Customer auth uses Supabase Auth in a dedicated project, separate from the research app's accounts. The collector schema moves to that project.
The dashboard is a Next.js app in dashboard/ in this repository, deployed as a second Vercel project.
The hierarchy is account, product, environment. A company is one account for now, because teams and roles are outside the MVP.
Each environment has a fixed type of production, beta, staging or dev, and a product has at most one of each, so production can be the default view.
features.evidence: 2026-11-01, hosted: the live collector now loads sites from the dedicated Supabase project. Hosted smoke checks passed (12 checks, 10/10 sessions revoked) using the existing ticket-app site, including bound verification with its unchanged secret. Each imported site's secret and origins were confirmed to match the previous live collector, and published SDK files match the frozen release. Locally, 108/108 tests pass, with the owner API suite also running through the real Postgres driver as the restricted role, covering isolation between customers and between environments. The first real customer account then created a product on the hosted service, which stored one production environment and its origins.

features.name: Signup, add product and install instructions
features.description: Self-service flow: sign up, add a product with its exact permitted origins, then copy script or package instructions for the chosen integration.
acceptance: Owners can sign up, sign in, recover their account and sign out without operator help.
Each environment gets a generated public installation identifier; any server credential is separate and labelled server-only.
Invalid or unapproved origins fail clearly.
Secrets never appear in the browser bundle or public snippet.
The DNS TXT check is implemented and tested, unverified domains are labelled, and a domain cannot have two verified owners.
No pre-populated customer account, site ID, key or domain allowlist ships with onboarding.
Secret rotation works without an outage, and revoke-now ends the old secret immediately.
Install instructions include a panel of setup instructions for a customer's coding agent, generated for that product and holding only public values.
decisions: Domain control uses a DNS TXT record and does not block events. A domain shows as unverified until the check passes, and each domain has one verified owner.
Rotation keeps the old secret working for 24 hours, with a separate revoke-now action for leaks. Secrets are shown once.

The default install puts nothing in front of visitors, at the owner's choice on 5 November: the customer's server reports signed requests and user-agent signals, and a script that draws nothing follows in SDK 0.6.0. The declaration widget stays in the docs as an opt-in that says every visitor sees it, and leaves the dashboard's snippets and the coding-agent instructions.
An install counts as receiving once the collector accepts a report from the customer's server, as well as when the widget loads.

The page script in SDK 0.6.0 is the default install's second part: one tag that draws nothing, sets no cookies and keeps a per-tab session in sessionStorage, shared with the widget. It records a page view on load and on each path change without a reload, and the browser's automation signals once per session. The widget's snippets leave page views to it, so a visit isn't counted twice.

Server reports join the page script's sessions through the page's response, at the owner's choice on 6 November: the server adds a random report ID to the response of a request it reported, and the page script reads it from the browser's timing data and joins that report to its session. No cookie is set. A first-party cookie, which would link more requests but can need visitors' consent, and keeping reports apart were the alternatives.

Its pages load and signed-out visitors are redirected. The collector reached Supabase's signing keys and rejected a forged token. features.name: Public site, docs and changelog
features.description: Give the product a public home: a landing page, documentation with a sidebar, search and on-page contents, and a changelog for releases and new features. The signed-in dashboard moves under /dashboard.
acceptance: / is a public landing page that explains what the product does and what it can't do.
/docs has a sidebar, search and on-page contents, and needs no sign-in.
/changelog lists releases and new features, one page per update, and needs no sign-in.
Docs and changelog posts are files in the repository, so a new post is a small pull request.
Products, analytics and settings move under /dashboard, and existing /products links redirect there.
Only /dashboard requires sign-in, and creating a product still requires an account.
Docs are also published in a form coding agents can read, such as llms.txt.
Docs keep the product's limits clear: a declaration is self-reported, not detection or verified identity.
decisions: The public site, docs and changelog live in the dashboard app, using Fumadocs.
Reading and learning need no account. Creating a product does, because a site ID must belong to someone.
The site can launch on its vercel.app address, and a custom domain can follow.

Signed-out visitors reach /dashboard only through sign-in, and a real signed-in session followed an old /products link to its product. Locally, 24/24 Playwright tests pass in Chromium and WebKit, and CI passed on the merged code. 2026-11-01, local: after the shared navbar, dark mode and demo page removal, ./init.sh --full passed with 108/108 collector, 4/4 dashboard unit, 48/48 SDK browser and 28/28 dashboard journey tests. Six before and after screenshots of /trial/ matched byte for byte. 2026-11-02, hosted: deployed the collector and dashboard from main at 1c8e3c2. The live home page has no demo button, the docs navbar lists the title, Docs and Changelog before the theme toggle and Dashboard, and signed-out /dashboard redirects to sign-in.

features.name: Installation connection check
features.description: Show real setup states driven by received events: waiting for installation, receiving events, or an actionable error.
acceptance: A real first event moves a product to receiving events.
Copying a snippet never shows a product as connected.
A failing installation shows an error the owner can act on.
decisions: Started before feat-003 was done, with the owner's approval, because it shows whether a real install works.
Status comes only from traffic the collector received: a widget load from an allowed origin, a declaration, or a refusal. Copying a snippet changes nothing.
The collector answers session preflights from any HTTPS or local origin, so a page on an unlisted origin can be traced to its site. The session request itself is still refused.
Refusals show for a week. Requests can claim any origin or secret, so the dashboard says what reached the collector, not who sent it.
features.evidence: 2026-11-02, local: ./init.sh --full passed with 118/118 collector, 5/5 dashboard unit, 48/48 SDK browser and 28/28 dashboard journey tests. Owner API tests run on memory, Postgres under the restricted app role and the production driver: a new product waits, reading it changes nothing, a widget load moves it to receiving events, a declaration is noted, refusals for an unlisted origin, a wrong secret and a bad binding context show only to their owner, a refused origin clears once allowed, and refusals are capped at 20 per site, noted once a minute and gone after a week. The browser journey shows Waiting for installation after copying the snippet, Receiving events after a real page load, and the refusal from a page on an unlisted origin. 2026-11-02, hosted: applied the install_activity migration to the production database after a dry run listed only that migration; the table has row-level security on and forced, and the app role has only its grants. Then deployed the collector and dashboard from main at 0790758. /health reports postgres, and a session preflight from an unlisted origin is answered while the session itself stays refused. npm run smoke:hosted passed 9 checks with 7/7 sessions revoked, and the production install_activity table then held loaded and declared rows for the operator test sites the smoke run used. The live dashboard shows Waiting for installation on a real customer product, which is correct: its site doesn't carry the snippet yet, so no customer product has been seen moving to Receiving events on the hosted site. Merged main passed 28/28 dashboard journey tests in Chromium and WebKit before the deploy.

features.name: Activity event contract
features.description: Extend the declaration model with repeatable activity events, so a declaration is one event type rather than the whole session timeline.
acceptance: The contract covers product, session, event ID and timestamp, with duplicate handling.
Independent signals keep their sources, and conflicting signals stay inspectable.
Agent name, provider claim and stated purpose are optional self-report, and unknown is valid.
The account reference is an opaque ID supplied by the host server and labelled as the account used, not as proof of delegation.
Action events distinguish attempted, rejected and application-confirmed outcomes, without arbitrary page or form contents.
src/protocol.ts and docs/protocol.md change together.
The change ships as a new versioned release and published v0.1.0 assets stay unchanged.
README and docs no longer state that page URLs are not collected.
decisions: Browser events carry the route path with query strings removed and ID-like segments masked. Hosts can supply their own route pattern, because masking only catches segments that look like IDs.
Server events carry a host-named action, opaque resource and account references, and an outcome.
Page titles, page text, form contents and raw IP addresses are never collected.
Customer activity data is kept for 30 days.
Started before feat-003 finished, with the owner's approval on 2 November 2026.

This feature defines the contract and stores it: the types, the path masking rule, an activity table kept 30 days with duplicate handling, declarations recorded as one event type, and an owner API to read a timeline. The browser and server producers of page views and actions are feat-006.
The v0.1.0 declaration export (GET /v1/events) is unchanged, and every declaration is also written to the timeline in the same statement.
Each feature that changes the SDK gets its own version, so a published version never changes whenever it is deployed. This one is 0.2.0, and install instructions move to it.
features.evidence: 2026-11-02, local: ./init.sh --full passed with 132/132 collector and contract tests, 5/5 dashboard unit, 48/48 SDK browser and 28/28 dashboard journey tests in Chromium and WebKit. Activity tests run on memory, Postgres under the restricted app role and the production driver: a declaration joins its session's timeline with the agent's own description, a retry with the same ID records once and a changed one conflicts, IDs are unique per site, a Person answer and host-reported actions stay side by side, events that break the contract are refused by both the collector and the database, and activity outlives its session's 7-day pruning until 30 days. The migration test shows declarations recorded before it join the timeline. Path masking, references, action names, outcomes and agent descriptions have unit tests. The 0.2.0 tarball passed the packed consumer check, and the frozen-release tests rebuild the exact published 0.1.0 bytes from its archived source. Deployed on 3 November in SDK 0.5.0, after its migrations reached the production database; 0.2.0 to 0.4.0 were never published. The hosted /health reports 0.5.0 and the published 0.1.0 files still match frozen.json.

features.name: Web Bot Auth verification
features.description: Verify requests that AI agents sign with Web Bot Auth (HTTP Message Signatures with a Signature-Agent key directory), so signing agents are identified by cryptographic evidence and visitors see nothing. The collector checks signatures reported by the customer's server or edge, and a customer whose CDN already checks them can report that verdict instead. It replaces the invisible widget the owner shelved.
acceptance: A customer's server or edge can report a request's signature headers with a plain HTTP call, and a Node helper does it in one line. Reporting never blocks or slows the visitor's response.

Signatures are checked against RFC 9421 and the current Web Bot Auth draft: the covered components include an @authority matching one of the product's origins and the Signature-Agent header, creation and expiry times are enforced, and keys come only from allowlisted key directories, cached for no longer than they are valid.
Spoofed, expired, replayed, tampered and wrong-authority signatures are rejected in tests, and a header that merely names a provider is never trusted.

A valid signature records a verified visit labelled with its signer. The label names the operator only, not the person or account it acts for. A failed check is recorded as an unverified claim with its reason.

A customer whose CDN already verifies Web Bot Auth, such as Cloudflare, Akamai or Vercel, can report that verdict instead. It counts only when the CDN sets it and strips any copy sent by the client, and each CDN is listed as supported only after a real request through it has been verified.
The owner sees verified and unverified signer visits for their product in the dashboard.
No signer is listed as supported until a real signed request from it has been verified on the hosted collector.
It ships as a new SDK version with docs/protocol.md updated, and published v0.1.0 assets stay unchanged.
decisions: The owner chose Web Bot Auth over the invisible widget on 2 November 2026. The widget is for agents and must never show to people, so no visible prompt goes on a real product.
The collector verifies signatures, so one tested implementation serves every backend. The customer's server forwards the headers, because browser code can't read them.
Key directories come from an allowlist of known signers. An unknown Signature-Agent is recorded as an unverified claim, never as verified.
A valid signature never blocks or admits a visitor; it only labels the visit.
The collector's own check ships first. CDN verdicts follow in this feature, because large customers often sit behind a CDN that already checks signatures.
Started straight after feat-005 at the owner's request to build the remaining features in order.

The verifier follows draft-ietf-webbotauth-httpsig-protocol-01 with Node's own crypto, no new dependency: Ed25519 and RSA-PSS-SHA512, keys matched by thumbprint, no redirects, and a key ID the cache doesn't know triggers one refetch at most every 10 seconds, for key rotation.
The local memory demo trusts a test signer on 127.0.0.1:4557 so the dashboard journey can show a real verified signature. The demo never runs in production.
This is SDK 0.3.0, and install instructions move to it.
features.evidence: 2026-11-02, local: ./init.sh --full passed with 143/143 collector and contract tests, 5/5 dashboard unit, 48/48 SDK browser and 28/28 dashboard journey tests in Chromium and WebKit. The draft's own Ed25519 test vector (draft-ietf-webbotauth-httpsig-protocol-01, appendix E.2.1) verifies, and its key ID is the key's RFC 8037 thumbprint. Tests with generated Ed25519 and RSA keys verify the dictionary and legacy Signature-Agent forms, and reject a signature for another allowed host, a wrong authority, expired, future and over-long windows, an unknown signer, an unpublished key, a different key under a published key ID, forged bytes, an uncovered Signature-Agent, another tag, a header that only names a provider, and an unreachable directory, each with its reason. The key directory honours Cache-Control, refuses redirects, wrong media types and non-200 answers, keeps keys through a failed refresh, drops keys outside nbf/exp, and refetches once for a rotated key at most every 10 seconds. The endpoint needs the site's secret, refuses browser requests and bad input, records a verified visit once per signature and a reused signature as a separate replay, and records a CDN verdict as cdn_reported. Signature events round-trip on memory, Postgres under the restricted role and the production driver, and the database refuses inconsistent ones. The Node helper skips unsigned requests without a network call, forwards only covered headers, works with Fetch and Node requests, and reports failures without throwing. In the dashboard journey, a request signed by a local test signer shows as Verified on the product page. Deployed on 3 November in SDK 0.5.0, after its migrations reached the production database; 0.2.0 to 0.4.0 were never published. Not yet done: no real signer or CDN has been verified on the hosted collector. 2026-11-04, hosted: the ticket app, now on SDK 0.5.0, forwards signed requests from its Next.js proxy with reportSignedRequest(). Two ChatGPT visits to its /login page, at 09:21 and 12:35 UTC, reached the proxy without signature headers, so nothing was recorded; ChatGPT most likely fetched those pages without its cloud browser. A probe with an oversized signature header was forwarded and refused with 400 as designed, and nothing was recorded. A temporary log in the proxy then showed ChatGPT Work's cloud browser loading /login at 13:05:20 UTC from Chrome 155, with sec-fetch-dest document, Signature, Signature-Input and Signature-Agent "https://chatgpt.com". The hosted collector recorded it at 13:05:21 as ChatGPT agent, verified, which makes ChatGPT Work's cloud browser the first supported signer. Not yet done: no CDN verdict has been verified on the hosted collector, and nobody has looked at this visit on the hosted dashboard's Signed agents card. 2026-11-04, local: the Signed agents docs' Next.js example was wrong. A minimal app with it, on Next.js 16.3.8 and the 0.5.0 tarball, answered 500 to every request, because middleware.ts runs in the Edge runtime and the server export needs node:crypto. Moved to proxy.ts, a request signed by the local test signer was recorded as wrong_authority under both next dev and next start, because Next changes the request URL's host to localhost. The corrected example rebuilds the URL from the Host header and passes it as url, and it was recorded as verified under next dev and next start, and on Next.js 15.5.28 with middleware.ts on the Node.js runtime under next start.

features.name: Browser and server activity collection
features.description: Collect access and activity evidence independently of whether a visitor answers the widget, through a browser integration and a server or edge integration.
acceptance: Visits and relevant actions are recorded for both answered and unanswered prompts.
Retries are idempotent.
Browser-supplied principal claims cannot become server-confirmed attribution.
Errors never appear as successful recording.
Logout, new-account and new-session boundaries work.
Behaviour is verified with the ticket app as an integration fixture, without coupling the repositories.
A non-Node backend can report actions with a plain HTTP request.
decisions: The first server integration is a plain HTTP events endpoint, so any backend can report actions without our package.
A Node helper sits on top of that endpoint. No paid dependency is required.
Started after feat-012 at the owner's request to build the remaining features in order.

Browser page views go to POST /v1/page-views with the visitor's own session token; the collector takes the session, origin and site from that session, masks the path again, and refuses any other field, so a browser can't attribute anything.

Server actions go to POST /v1/actions with the site's secret. An action joins a session only through the host's own session binding, hashed like a binding context, never a session ID a browser could have supplied.
The widget records one page view per page load once its session is ready, and again after reset; pageView() covers apps that change pages without reloading, and data-page-views="off" turns it off.
GET /v1/activity lets a site's server export its activity with its secret, like the declaration export.
This is SDK 0.4.0, and install instructions move to it.
features.evidence: 2026-11-02, local: ./init.sh --full passed with 153/153 collector, contract and SDK unit tests, 5/5 dashboard unit, 54/54 SDK browser and 28/28 dashboard journey tests in Chromium and WebKit. In real browsers each page load records one page view before any answer, a reload adds another to the same session, a reset starts the new session with its own, a failed page view retries with the same ID and is recorded once, and data-page-views="off" sends none. Collector tests show the path is masked by the collector, a retry is a duplicate and a changed retry a conflict, a browser can't send accountRef, a session ID or any other field, a revoked or foreign-origin session is refused, and preflight works. Server actions need the site's secret, refuse browser requests and bad input, link to a session only through the host's binding (including after signing out and in as someone else), are recorded once on retry, and work from a plain HTTP request. The binding lookup passes on memory, Postgres under the restricted role and the production driver. reportAction() retries with the same ID, never throws, and only reports recorded when confirmed; the widget's pageView() rejects and reports unless the collector confirms that view. Deployed on 3 November in SDK 0.5.0, after its migrations reached the production database; 0.2.0 to 0.4.0 were never published. Not yet done: the ticket app still installs SDK 0.1.0 from the hosted tarball, so the integration fixture waits for it to move to 0.5.0. 2026-11-04, hosted: the ticket app moved to SDK 0.5.0, installed from the hosted 0.5.0 tarball with the integrity in release.json, and was deployed to production. Its proxy forwards signed requests, and the hosted collector verified a ChatGPT cloud browser visit through it (see feat-012). Not yet checked through it: page views and server actions on 0.5.0. 2026-11-04, local integration: the ticket app (ticket-management#4) now reports each package-run ticket save with reportAction(). The report is sent after the response, joined through the app's package session binding, and reuses the save's audit event ID. The app's browser smoke check passed all 15 scenarios in Chromium and in WebKit against the local collector, reading the collector's activity export with the site's secret. An unanswered optional run's collector session held 2 page views and its save as a confirmed action, with no declaration. A declared required run's session held 3 page views, the declaration, the blocked direct write as rejected and the accepted save as confirmed (Chromium counts). A new run got a new collector session. Not yet run: the same smoke check against the hosted collector, which needs the owner's research login.

features.name: Product-owner dashboard
features.description: Overview, recent-session list with date and product filters, and session timeline built on real collected data for one environment at a time, showing provenance and coverage limits in plain language.
acceptance: An external tester can install the integration and find their own test session without an operator query or private database access.
Counts reconcile with event records, and requests, sessions and completed actions are counted separately.
Retries, asset requests and client/server duplicates do not inflate counts, and a session with both a verified provider and a self-declaration is not double-counted.
Customer isolation holds at the API as well as the UI.
Empty, loading, disconnected and error states are covered.
Unclassified sessions stay unknown and are never labelled human.
Every signal stays visible, and conflicting signals are shown rather than resolved.
An environment switcher defaults to production and keeps the choice in the URL, and each environment's analytics are shown separately.
Customers can add an environment and copy its snippet from the dashboard.
decisions: Sessions show Verified signer, Declared AI, Declared person, Suspected automation or Unknown, with no numeric score.
Side-by-side environment comparison is out of scope for the MVP.
Started after feat-006 at the owner's request to build the remaining features in order.

Label precedence is Verified signer, Declared AI, Suspected automation, Declared person, then Unknown: a signature outranks what a visitor says, a self-declared agent outranks heuristics, and heuristics outrank a Person answer, which never erases them. Conflicts are listed, never resolved.
Counts are computed by the collector from the event records themselves, from at most the latest 10,000 events in a period, and the page says when a period is busier than that.
features.evidence: 2026-11-02, local: ./init.sh --full passed with 158/158 collector tests, 5/5 dashboard unit, 54/54 SDK browser and 30/30 dashboard journey tests in Chromium and WebKit. Analytics tests run real events through a store: a retried page view counts once, page views reconcile with their events, a session with both a verified signature and a Person answer counts once as Verified signer with the conflict listed, prefer-not-to-say and signal-less sessions stay Unknown, no label is ever human, and actions and signed requests without a session are counted apart. The analytics route passes on memory, Postgres under the restricted role and the production driver, keeps environments apart, refuses an unknown range, and returns 404 to another customer. In the browser journey, a customer opens Activity from the product page and sees one session, one page view and one verified signed request without a session, then the session's timeline with each event and who vouches for it. Another journey adds a staging environment from the product page, sees its secret once, opens it from a link that keeps it in the URL, copies a snippet with a different site ID, and sees Staging's own empty and not-yet-installed states, a 30-day period and a refused session lookup. Previewed locally with sample activity. Deployed to the hosted collector and dashboard on 3 November. 2026-11-04, local: the error state now has a browser test. Next's Playwright test mode aborts the dashboard server's analytics request for that test only, after the product has loaded. Activity says the collector didn't answer and offers Try again, with no counts or empty state in its place, and Try again loads the 30-day period once the collector answers. Test mode is on for next dev only, never in a production build. ./init.sh --full passed with 187/187 tests, 5/5 dashboard unit, 56/56 SDK browser tests, the dashboard build and 34/34 dashboard journey tests in Chromium and WebKit. The journey shows a new account installing and finding its own session without operator access; a real external tester's run is part of the pilot onboarding in feat-010.

features.name: Heuristic automation signals
features.description: Add heuristic automation signals one at a time as evidence for traffic that doesn't sign, and test what each contributes. Signed-agent verification, including CDN verdicts, is feat-012.
acceptance: Ordinary automation is not labelled an AI agent.
A heuristic signal is shown as evidence with its source, never as verified identity.
A self-declaration is never promoted to verified identity, and a Person answer does not erase contradictory evidence.
No numerical confidence score ships without a defensible meaning and validation.
decisions: Web Bot Auth and CDN signed-agent verdicts moved to feat-012, so verified identity can ship before the heuristics.
A heuristic signal never blocks a visitor.
Labels follow the evidence in feat-007.
Started after feat-007 at the owner's request to build the remaining features in order.

The first signals are a webdriver flag and a headless browser from the page, and a user agent that names an AI agent or crawler from the server. The page's signals are opt-in, because they collect something new.
A signal never makes a session verified or Declared AI. A session whose strongest evidence is a signal is Suspected automation, and a Person answer next to one is a conflict.
This is SDK 0.5.0, and install instructions move to it.

The page script in SDK 0.6.0 reports the page's signals by default, superseding the opt-in above for that script only, because the owner's 5 November choice was a script that records page views and automation signals. data-automation-signals="off" turns them off, and the widget's stay opt-in.
features.evidence: 2026-11-02, local: ./init.sh --full passed with 166/166 collector, contract and SDK unit tests, 5/5 dashboard unit, 56/56 SDK browser and 30/30 dashboard journey tests in Chromium and WebKit. User agents naming an AI agent or crawler, and HeadlessChrome, are read as signals; an ordinary Chrome user agent and a token inside another word are not. A page can report only webdriver or a headless browser from its own session, a server can also report a user agent's claim linked through its binding, and the server helper skips ordinary and asset requests without a network call and reports failures without throwing. Signals round-trip on memory, Postgres under the restricted role and the production driver, and the database refuses a page reporting a user agent claim, a signal without a kind, and signals with other events' fields. In the analytics, a webdriver flag or a user agent claim labels a session Suspected automation, never Verified signer or Declared AI; a self-declared AI still outranks a signal; and a Person answer next to a signal is labelled by the signal with the conflict listed. The widget sends no signals by default; with automationSignals on, a real automated Chromium and WebKit each report webdriver once, as browser_reported. Firefox doesn't launch locally, so its run of the new browser test is left to CI. What each signal contributes with real traffic is validation work for feat-009. Deployed to the hosted collector and dashboard on 3 November. 2026-11-06, local: the page script reports webdriver and headless_browser once per session, marked with the session in sessionStorage so a reload doesn't repeat them. A browser journey found a repeat on reload, which this fixed, and unit tests and journeys in Chromium and WebKit cover it. Not yet deployed.

features.name: Controlled validation
features.description: Run the pilot acceptance work against a frozen, documented test matrix.
acceptance: The matrix covers cooperative agents, silent agents, agents choosing Person, ordinary scripted automation, humans and mixed human/agent sessions.
Tests cover API-only access, JavaScript-disabled clients, denied actions and abandoned visits.
Missed agents, false positives, attribution errors, task outcome and coverage are reported separately.
The real model, browser, control method and any assistance are recorded.
Small successful batches are reported as exploratory, not as proof of universal reliability.
All three hard rules hold across the test matrix.
decisions: Three hard rules apply now: no customer sees another's data, no self-report is shown as verified, and no unknown session is labelled human.
Detection targets are set after a small baseline run and frozen before the measured pilot.

The owner's 90–100% identification goal is measured against agents we run ourselves across the test matrix, decided on 5 November: signed cloud browsers, agents in a person's own browser, API clients and scripted automation. Each kind is reported separately, so a result names the agent and how it ran. The owner agrees the numeric targets after the baseline run.

features.name: External-test release
features.description: Prepare a documented pilot: run package, HTTP, database, tenant-isolation, browser and hosted checks, then verify onboarding with a new account and a new product.
acceptance: All checks pass against the deployed target, not only local builds.
The onboarding journey is verified with a new account and a new product.
Concise install, uninstall and troubleshooting instructions exist.
Retention is defined, and deletion and cleanup are tested.
Release claims stay limited to a documented pilot, not enterprise procurement, compliance, universal detection or verified delegation.
decisions: Started after feat-008 at the owner's request to build the remaining features in order.

Deleting a product is a soft delete, at the owner's request on 3 November: the product is hidden and its sites stop at once, and the owner can restore it for 30 days, matching how long activity is kept. After that the prune, or Delete now, removes it and everything its sites recorded in one SQL statement, so a product is never gone while its data stays. The app role gains delete on products and environments for that, and update on deleted_at.
The owner runs the hosted onboarding check with a new account, because agents don't create accounts on the hosted app.
features.evidence: 2026-11-03, local: ./init.sh --full passed with 175/175 collector, contract and SDK unit tests, 5/5 dashboard unit, 56/56 SDK browser and 32/32 dashboard journey tests in Chromium and WebKit. On memory, Postgres under the restricted role and the production driver: deleting a product hides it and its staging environment from every owner route and refuses new sessions on both sites while keeping what they recorded; another customer gets 404 for delete, restore and the deleted list; restoring brings back the same site IDs and sites that accept sessions again, and a second restore gets 404; past 30 days the product leaves the deleted list and can't be restored; restoring at the 25-product limit gets 409; a live product can't be removed for good; Delete now and the prune each remove a deleted product with every session, declaration, activity event and install note its site recorded, while another product keeps its data. In the browser journey, deleting needs the product's exact name, the product moves to Recently deleted, Restore brings it back, and Delete now removes it after a confirmation. Install, troubleshooting and uninstall instructions, the retention rules and what the pilot may and may not claim are in the docs and docs/pilot.md.
